Chapter 2 · Series expansions: two ways to expand the signal

© 2026 Chantal Tax. All rights reserved. Shared for viewing only; not licensed for reuse or redistribution. Course: simulating the diffusion MRI signal. Chapter 1 set up the eigenmodes and the Bloch–Torrey equation. This chapter turns them into the signal. What you'll take away
  1. The Bloch–Torrey equation as a matrix equation in the eigenmodes of Chapter 1: the modes stay the same, the gradient only couples them.
  2. How to compute the signal exactly for any gradient waveform: Grebenkov's MCF and the multiple propagator, and the error each makes.
  3. How many modes you need, and why.
  4. The cumulant expansion of the signal, with the Gaussian phase approximation as its first term, built from the mode weights of Chapter 1.
  5. Why finite gradient pulses change the meaning of the measured ||(D||) and ||(K||).
  6. How the two series are connected: every cumulant is a product of the same matrices.
  7. How far the cumulant series reaches (its radius of convergence, set by the nearest complex zero of the signal), and how to compute cumulants of any order in practice.
Every exercise has hints and a worked answer, folded away. Try the exercise first, then open the hint, then the answer.

The course at a glance

Ch Topic Status

2 Series expansions: (a) the eigenmodes coupled by the gradient, i.e. matrix methods; (b) the cumulant expansion in powers of the gradient; (c) how the two connect this notebook
3 Analytical formulas: the PGSE box, the narrow-pulse ||((q,t)||) map, the long-pulse ||((g,T)||) map, the inside of the box, relaxing walls and exchange next
4 Grids and meshes: the method of lines, finite differences, time stepping and stability, periodic cells, finite elements, curved walls done
5 Monte Carlo: simulating the random walk coming
Units: lengths in µm, times in ms, gradients in mT/m. In this chapter ||(D = 2||) µm²/ms throughout. All examples use a slab of width ||(L||) with the gradient across it: its modes are known in closed form, so every number can be checked by hand. Cylinders and spheres work the same way with the modes from the Chapter 1 tables.

Two kinds of series

Both halves of this chapter expand the signal in a series. They are easy to confuse, and they do very different things.
2a · Eigenmode expansion (matrix methods) 2b · Cumulant expansion

Section 2c shows that they are built from the same pieces.

2a · Matrix methods

The Bloch–Torrey equation in the eigenbasis

The eigenmodes of a pore are a complete set: any magnetization that satisfies the interface conditions can be written as a sum of them. So write ||[m(x,t) = \sum_n c_n(t)\,u_n(x).||]Putting this into Bloch–Torrey turns one partial differential equation into a set of ordinary ones, one per mode: ||[\frac{d\mathbf c}{dt} = -\big(D\Lambda + i\gamma\,g(t)\,\mathbf B\big)\,\mathbf c,\qquad \Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\dots),\qquad B_{nm} = \int u_n(x)\,x\,u_m(x)\,dx .||]
  • The modes do not change. They are the modes of the pore from Chapter 1, fixed by its shape and interface conditions. The gradient does not create new ones.
  • Diffusion is diagonal. On its own, each mode decays at its own rate ||(D\lambda_n||).
  • The gradient couples the modes. The field ||(x||) is not a mode, so multiplying a mode by ||(x||) spreads it over the others; ||(\mathbf B||) says how much goes where. All the geometry is in ||(\Lambda||) and ||(\mathbf B||).
  • Start and finish. Spins start uniform, ||(m(x,0) = u_0||), so ||(\mathbf c(0) = \mathbf e_0 = (1,0,0,\dots)||). Only the uniform mode has a nonzero integral, so the signal is just the first component at the echo: ||(E = c_0(T)||).
||(\mathbf B||) is the position matrix of Chapter 1 (Exercise 5): real, symmetric, nonzero only between modes of opposite parity, with couplings that fall off as ||(1/n^2||), and ||(B_{0n}^2||) equal to the MSD weights. Together, ||(\Lambda||) and ||(\mathbf B||) are everything the geometry contributes. The whole simulation problem is now: propagate ||(\mathbf c||) from ||(\mathbf e_0||) to the echo, and read off ||(c_0||). The methods below differ only in how they step through time.

data.text/markdown:
The PGSE signal with Grebenkov's MCF

When the gradient is constant over an interval of length ||(\tau||), ||(d\mathbf c/dt = -(D\Lambda + i\gamma g\mathbf B)\mathbf c||) has constant coefficients and is solved by one matrix exponential: ||(\mathbf c(t+\tau) = e^{-(D\Lambda + i\gamma g\mathbf B)\tau}\,\mathbf c(t)||). A PGSE sequence is piecewise constant: a lobe of ||(+G||) for ||(\delta||), no gradient for ||(\Delta - \delta||), and a second lobe. The refocusing pulse flips the phase, which is the same as flipping the sign of the second lobe (the "effective gradient"). So the exact signal is a product of three matrices, sandwiched between the uniform mode: ||[E = \Big[\,e^{-(D\Lambda - i\gamma G\mathbf B)\,\delta}\;e^{-D\Lambda(\Delta-\delta)}\;e^{-(D\Lambda + i\gamma G\mathbf B)\,\delta}\,\Big]_{00}.||]This is the MCF method in the form of Grebenkov (2007), building on Barzykin (1999). It is exact for any piecewise-constant waveform; the only approximation is the number of modes ||(N||) kept. Read the product from right to left: that is the order in time. Move the sliders: the same sliders drive every figure in this chapter.

data.text/markdown:
Any waveform: a staircase, or diffusion and kicks in turn

Real gradients have ramps: the lobes are trapezoids, and oscillating or free waveforms are not piecewise constant at all. There are two ways to step through such a waveform with the same ||(\Lambda||) and ||(\mathbf B||). 1 · Staircase MCF. Replace each ramp by ||(K||) short constant steps (at the midpoint value) and multiply their exact exponentials (Barzykin 1999; Grebenkov 2007). Each step costs a full ||(N\times N||) matrix exponential, because ||(D\Lambda||) and ||(\mathbf B||) do not commute. 2 · Multiple propagator. Cut the whole sequence into ||(M||) steps of length ||(\tau||) and, within each step, separate diffusion from dephasing: half a step of diffusion, a phase kick, half a step of diffusion, ||[\mathbf c \;\leftarrow\; e^{-D\Lambda\tau/2}\;e^{-i\gamma g\,\tau\,\mathbf B}\;e^{-D\Lambda\tau/2}\;\mathbf c .||]Diffusion is diagonal, so ||(e^{-D\Lambda\tau/2}||) is just a list of numbers. The kick is diagonal in the eigenbasis of ||(\mathbf B||), which you diagonalise once. So a step costs only two matrix–vector products. This is the multiple (narrow-pulse) propagator of Caprihan et al. (1996) and Callaghan (1997), in the symmetric splitting of Strang (1968). Callaghan writes the kick in the position basis as the matrix ||(A_{nm}(q) = \int u_n e^{-iqx} u_m||), with ||(q = \gamma g\tau||): the same thing. Both methods are second order: halving the step divides the error by four. The figure checks this on a trapezoidal PGSE.

data.text/markdown:
How many modes? Smoothness, and Jackson's theorem

How large must ||(N||) be? Approximation theory gives the right way to think about it. The idea. The slab's modes are cosines. A sum of ||(N||) of them is a truncated Fourier series of the magnetization mirrored at both walls (its even, periodic extension). Jackson's theorems (Jackson 1911) bound how well ||(N||) terms can approximate a function by how smooth it is: if the mirrored function has ||(k||) continuous derivatives, the best error falls at least as fast as ||(N^{-k}||) (times a measure of how smoothly the ||(k||)-th derivative varies). Bernstein's theorems (Bernstein 1912) give the converse, and for analytic functions the convergence is exponential. In short: smoothness of the mirrored function sets the speed of convergence. Mirroring is what makes the wall behaviour matter. A function with a nonzero slope at a wall gets a kink when mirrored, even if it is perfectly smooth inside. The left panel shows the cosine coefficients of four functions:
  • a step (a jump): coefficients fall as ||(1/n||);
  • the gradient field ||(x||) itself: slope 1 at the walls, so the mirror has kinks, and the coefficients fall as ||(1/n^2||). These are the couplings ||(B_{0n}||) of Chapter 1, Exercise 5;
  • a smooth step with zero slope at the walls: the first jump is in the third derivative of the mirror, so ||(1/n^4||);
  • the propagator at ||(t > 0||): diffusion has smoothed it completely, and the coefficients ||(e^{-D\lambda_n t}u_n(x_0)||) fall faster than any power.
And the Bloch–Torrey equation? Diffusion smooths, but the gradient keeps feeding in the field ||(x||), which does not fit the walls. Differentiate the equation once in ||(x||) and evaluate it at a wall, where ||(\partial m/\partial x = 0||) at all times: you find ||(\partial^3 m/\partial x^3 = i\gamma g\, m/D \ne 0||). So the mirrored magnetization has a jump in its third derivative, and the convergence in ||(N||) is algebraic, not exponential. The right panel shows it for the PGSE above: the error in ||(E||) falls roughly as ||(N^{-5}||). That is steep enough that 10–20 modes give 6–8 correct digits at moderate gradients.

data.text/markdown:
Practical rules for choosing ||(N||)
  1. Resolve the finest length scale in ||(m||). Mode ||(n||) has a wavelength of about ||(2L/n||), so you need ||(N \gtrsim||) a few ||(\times L/(\pi\ell)||), where ||(\ell||) is the smallest of ||(\sqrt{D\,t}||) for the shortest relevant time and the gradient length ||(\ell_g = (D/\gamma g)^{1/3}||).
  2. Damping must beat dephasing in the last mode kept (Grebenkov's criterion, Grebenkov 2007, Sec. VI.A): ||(D\lambda_N \gg \gamma g L||).
  3. Always check: double ||(N||) and see whether ||(E||) changes in the digits you care about.
In 2D and 3D the number of modes below a given ||(\lambda||) grows as ||(\lambda^{d/2}||) (Weyl's law, 1912), so the same resolution costs about ||((L/\ell)^d||) modes. A linear gradient couples only modes whose angular orders differ by one, which keeps cylinders and spheres cheap.

2b · The cumulant expansion

Expanding the logarithm of the signal

The path picture gives ||(E = \langle e^{-i\varphi}\rangle||): the characteristic function of the phase. As for the displacement in Chapter 1, its logarithm is a series of cumulants: ||[\ln E = \sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-i)^n}{n!}\,\kappa_n(\varphi) = -\frac12\langle\varphi^2\rangle + \frac1{24}\Big(\langle\varphi^4\rangle - 3\langle\varphi^2\rangle^2\Big) - \dots||]The odd cumulants vanish for a refocused echo in a symmetric pore (the phase is as likely to be ||(+\varphi||) as ||(-\varphi||)). Since ||(\varphi \propto g||), this is a series in powers of the gradient: ||(\kappa_2 \propto g^2||), ||(\kappa_4 \propto g^4||), and so on. The Gaussian phase approximation (GPA) keeps only the first term: ||(E \approx e^{-\langle\varphi^2\rangle/2}||). It is exact when the phase is Gaussian (free diffusion, Exercise 4), and good whenever the higher cumulants are small compared with ||(\langle\varphi^2\rangle||).

The second cumulant from the modes

||(\varphi = \gamma\int g(t)\,x(t)\,dt||) is linear in the path, so its variance only needs the position autocorrelation: ||[\langle\varphi^2\rangle = \gamma^2\iint g(t_1)\,g(t_2)\,\langle x(t_1)\,x(t_2)\rangle\,dt_1\,dt_2 .||]In a pore, with spins starting uniformly and ||(x||) measured from the centre, the propagator of Chapter 1 gives ||[\langle x(t_1)\,x(t_2)\rangle = \sum_{n\ge1} B_{0n}^2\; e^{-D\lambda_n|t_1-t_2|}.||]So the GPA needs only two lists per geometry: the weights ||(w_n = B_{0n}^2||) and the rates ||(D\lambda_n||). For the slab they are the MSD weights ||(8L^2/(n\pi)^4||) and ||(D(n\pi/L)^2||). Each mode contributes a double integral of the waveform against one exponential, which you can do once and for all for a PGSE (Murday & Cotts 1968; Neuman 1974; for any waveform, Stepišnik 1993 and van Gelderen et al. 1994).

The fourth cumulant: kurtosis, and why finite pulses matter

Diffusion kurtosis imaging (Jensen et al. 2005) fits the first two terms in powers of ||(b||): ||[\ln E = -b\,D_{\text{app}} + \frac16\,b^2D_{\text{app}}^2K_{\text{app}} + O(b^3).||]With narrow pulses (||(\delta \to 0||)), the phase is ||(-q||) times the displacement ||(X||) (Chapter 3 derives this), and ||(b = q^2\Delta||). Then ||(D_{\text{app}}||) and ||(K_{\text{app}}||) are exactly the displacement cumulants of Chapter 1: ||(D(\Delta)||) and ||(K(\Delta)||). With finite pulses they are not. During a pulse the spin keeps moving, so the phase records a time-averaged position during each lobe, not the end points. The signal becomes the Fourier transform of a "centre-of-mass" propagator, and isolated pores look smaller than they are (Mitra & Halperin 1995). The measured cumulants are then time integrals of the multi-time correlation functions ||(\langle x(t_1)x(t_2)\rangle||), ||(\langle x(t_1)x(t_2)x(t_3)x(t_4)\rangle||), … weighted by the waveform. The figure extracts ||(D_{\text{app}}||) and ||(K_{\text{app}}||) from the exact signal (MCF, a polynomial fit of ||(\ln E||) in ||(b||) at small ||(b||)) and compares them with the displacement values of Chapter 1.

data.text/markdown:
The same in frequency: the diffusion spectrum

Write the variance of the phase in the frequency domain. With ||(Q(\omega) = \int q(t)\,e^{i\omega t}dt||), ||[\langle\varphi^2\rangle = \frac2\pi\int_0^\infty |Q(\omega)|^2\,\mathcal D(\omega)\,d\omega ,||]where ||(\mathcal D(\omega)||) is the diffusion spectrum, the Fourier transform of the velocity autocorrelation (Stepišnik 1993). The gradient waveform acts as a filter ||(|Q(\omega)|^2||) that picks which frequencies of the motion are seen. For free diffusion ||(\mathcal D(\omega) = D||) at every frequency and Parseval gives back ||(2bD||). For a pore, the modes give ||[\mathcal D(\omega) = \sum_{n\ge1} w_n\,D\lambda_n\,\frac{\omega^2}{(D\lambda_n)^2 + \omega^2},||]which rises from 0 (no long-range motion in a closed pore) to ||(D||) (at high frequency the walls are not felt). Oscillating gradients (OGSE) have ||(|Q|^2||) peaked at their frequency, so they sample ||(\mathcal D(\omega)||) there: high frequencies probe short times.

The two halves of this chapter look different, but they are built from the same ||(\Lambda||) and ||(\mathbf B||). Expand the exact solution of 2a in powers of the gradient. Treating ||(i\gamma g\mathbf B||) as a perturbation of ||(D\Lambda||) (variation of constants, applied repeatedly): ||[c_0(T) = 1 \;-\; i\gamma\int_0^T g(t)\,B_{00}\,dt \;-\; \gamma^2\int_0^T\!dt_2\int_0^{t_2}\!dt_1\;g(t_2)\,g(t_1)\,\big[\mathbf B\,e^{-D\Lambda(t_2-t_1)}\mathbf B\big]_{00} \;+\;\dots||]The ||(n||)-th term holds ||(n||) factors of ||(\mathbf B||) separated by diffusion propagators. Each such sandwich is a multi-time correlation function of the position, ||[\big[\mathbf B\,e^{-D\Lambda(t_2-t_1)}\mathbf B\big]_{00} = \langle x(t_1)\,x(t_2)\rangle,\qquad \big[\mathbf B e^{-D\Lambda\tau_3}\mathbf B e^{-D\Lambda\tau_2}\mathbf B e^{-D\Lambda\tau_1}\mathbf B\big]_{00} = \langle x(t_1)\,x(t_2)\,x(t_3)\,x(t_4)\rangle,\ \dots||]which is where the name of the method comes from: MCF = multiple correlation function (Grebenkov 2007). The time-ordered exponential of Axelrod & Sen (2001) is the same expansion written compactly.
  • The moments of the phase are these terms. Taking the logarithm turns them into cumulants: the second-order term is ||(-\langle\varphi^2\rangle/2||), the GPA.
  • The matrix methods of 2a sum the whole series at once, by computing the exponentials directly. That is why they work at any ||(G||).
  • The cumulant series of 2b truncates the logarithm. That is why it has a radius of convergence (Exercise 5c), while the series for ||(E||) itself does not (for a finite number of modes).

How far does the cumulant series reach? The radius of convergence, and computing it in practice

Exercises 5c and 7c showed that the cumulant series stops somewhere. This section shows where, and how to compute the cumulants of any order in practice. The radius of convergence. ||(\ln E(G)||) is analytic wherever ||(E\ne0||), so its power series around ||(G = 0||) converges inside the largest disc that contains no zero of ||(E||). Two symmetries place the zeros:
  • ||(E||) is even in ||(G||): reversing the gradient is the same as mirroring the slab. So ||(\ln E||) is a series in ||(G^2||), i.e. in ||(b||).
  • ||(E||) is real for real ||(G||) (a symmetric pore), so ||(E(\bar G) = \overline{E(G)}||).
→ Zeros come in fours, ||(\pm G^*||) and ||(\pm\bar G^*||), and the radius is ||(R = \lvert G^*\rvert||), the modulus of the nearest one. In ||(b||)-units, ||(b^* = \gamma^2\lvert G^*\rvert^2\delta^2(\Delta - \delta/3)||). What the zero does to the coefficients. Write ||(\ln E = \sum_k c_{2k}G^{2k}||). Close to its nearest zeros, ||(\ln E||) behaves like ||(\ln(1 - G^2/G^{*2}) + \ln(1 - G^2/\bar G^{*2})||) plus a part that is analytic in a larger disc. Expanding ||(\ln(1-u) = -\sum_k u^k/k||) gives, for large ||(k||) (Darboux 1878), ||[c_{2k}\approx-\frac2k\,\lvert G^*\rvert^{-2k}\cos(2k\theta^*),\qquad \theta^* = \arg G^* .||]→ The coefficients shrink like ||(R^{-2k}||): the cumulant series behaves like a geometric series in ||((G/R)^2||). Truncating it after the ||(G^{2K}||) term leaves an error of order ||((G/R)^{2K+2}/K||). That is tiny for ||(G\ll R||) and useless near ||(R||), however many terms you keep. Three ways to get the cumulants
Route How Strength Weakness
Fit a polynomial in ||(b||) to ||(\ln E||) DKI-style, on ||([0, b_{\max}]||) works on measured data biased by the omitted higher terms; ill-conditioned beyond 2–3 terms
Nested time integrals (2c) ||(k||)-fold integrals of ||(\mathbf Be^{-D\Lambda\tau}\mathbf B\cdots||) exact, and each term has a meaning the cost grows fast with the order; impractical beyond the 4th
Cauchy integral on a circle ||(E||) at ||(M||) complex ||(G||) on a circle, then an FFT of ||(\ln E||) every order at once, to rounding error; also reveals ||(R||) needs a model that accepts complex ||(G||)
Recipe: cumulants from a circle in the complex plane (Lyness & Moler 1967) ① Find the nearest zero ||(G^*||). Look for a dip of ||(\lvert E\rvert||) along real ||(G||), or for dark spots of ||(\lvert E\rvert||) in the complex plane, and refine with Newton's method in complex ||(G||). The MCF needs no change for a complex ||(G||): it is the same matrix exponential. ② Choose a circle inside the disc, ||(r < R||) (here ||(r = 0.7R||)), with ||(M||) points ||(G_j = r\,e^{2\pi ij/M}||) (||(M = 64||)). ③ Compute ||(\ln E(G_j)||) with its phase unwrapped along the circle. ④ FFT: ||(c_k = \mathrm{FFT}(\ln E)_k\big/(M\,r^k)||). This is the trapezoidal rule for Cauchy's integral ||(c_k = \frac1{2\pi i}\oint\ln E(G)\,G^{-k-1}dG||). On a circle it converges geometrically, with an error of order ||((r/R)^M||) (Trefethen & Weideman 2014). ⑤ Check: ||(c_0\approx0||) (since ||(E(0) = 1||)) and all odd ||(c_k\approx0||). If the circle encloses a zero, the unwrapped phase does not return to its start: it gains ||(2\pi||) per zero inside (the argument principle), and both checks fail. ⑥ Convert. With ||(b = \beta G^2||) and ||(\beta = \gamma^2\delta^2(\Delta-\delta/3)||): ||(\ D_{\text{app}} = -c_2/\beta||) and ||(K_{\text{app}} = 6c_4/(\beta^2D_{\text{app}}^2)||), and so on for the higher orders.
